title: Caedes nocturna. Mors Nisi et Euryali
titleEn: The Night Raid and the Deaths of Nisus and Euryalus — Aeneid IX.314–445
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Nisus and Euryalus slip out over the Trojan trenches and into the Rutulian lines, where the enemy lies sprawled in drunken sleep among chariots, weapons and wine. Nisus cuts a road through them while Euryalus keeps watch, and then both kill: Rhamnes, a king and Turnus's augur, who could not foresee his own death; Remus and his attendants; young Serranus, who had gambled half the night away; and a crowd of nameless men. Nisus sees that they are being carried away by slaughter and greed and calls a halt before dawn. They leave much of the plunder, but Euryalus takes Rhamnes's medallions and golden belt and puts on the helmet of Messapus. Three hundred Latin horsemen under Volcens, riding with messages for Turnus, catch the gleam of that helmet in the moonlight. In a dark and tangled wood the two are separated; Nisus gets clear, turns back for his friend, and sees him taken. He prays to the Moon and kills two of the horsemen with spears thrown from the dark. Volcens, unable to find the thrower, turns his sword on Euryalus, and Nisus breaks cover crying that the deed was all his own — too late. Euryalus dies like a flower cut by the plough, and Nisus, forcing his way to Volcens, kills him and falls dead on his friend's body. The raid is Virgil's rewriting of Iliad 10, where Diomedes and Odysseus slaughter the sleeping Thracians and come home safe with King Rhesus's horses; these raiders do not come home.
part: The Night Raid and the Deaths of Nisus and Euryalus (IX.314–445)

sentences.t:
Egressi superant fossas noctisque per umbram
castra inimica petunt, multis tamen ante futuri
exitio.
sentences.l:
Having gone out, they get over the trenches, and through the shadow of night
the hostile camp they seek — to many, however, before that, destined to be
a destruction.
sentences.i: Out they went and over the trenches, making through the darkness of night for the enemy camp — and yet, before their own end, they were to be the ruin of many.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. The last part ended with Ascanius's messages for his father scattered by the winds (9.312–313); now the two are out of the gate. 'Egressi', 'having gone out', from 'egredior'. 'superant fossas', 'they get over the ditches', the trenches round the Trojan camp. 'castra inimica', the Rutulian camp that rings the Trojans. 'multis… futuri exitio', 'about to be a destruction to many', the double dative ('multis' the persons affected, 'exitio' what they will be to them) with the future participle of 'sum'; 'tamen ante', 'yet first', before they die themselves: the poet tells us at the outset how it will end. Elision 'castr(a) inimica'.

sentences.t:
Passim somno vinoque per herbam
corpora fusa vident, arrectos litore currus,
inter lora rotasque viros, simul arma iacere,
vina simul.
sentences.l:
Everywhere, by sleep and wine, across the grass
bodies poured out they see, tilted up on the shore chariots,
among reins and wheels men, at the same time arms lying,
wine at the same time.
sentences.i: Everywhere they saw bodies sprawled on the grass in drunken sleep, chariots tipped up on the river-bank, men lying among the reins and wheels, weapons scattered about, and wine with them.
sentences.n: 'Passim', 'here and there', all about. 'somno vinoque… fusa', 'poured out by sleep and wine', sprawled: Nisus's report (9.236–237) proves true. 'vident' takes plain accusatives ('corpora fusa', 'arrectos… currus') and then accusatives with the infinitive 'iacere', 'lie', which serves 'viros', 'arma' and 'vina' alike, as the eye moves from thing to thing. 'arrectos… currus', 'chariots tilted up', tipped back with their poles in the air once the horses are unyoked; 'litore', 'on the shore', probably the river-bank. 'simul… simul', 'together… together', arms and wine side by side, the whole carelessness of the camp in one picture. In Iliad 10 Diomedes and Odysseus find the Thracians asleep in the same way, but with their armour laid in good order beside them and each man's horses by him (10.471–475); Virgil's Rutulians lie in disorder. No elisions.

sentences.t: Prior Hyrtacides sic ore locutus:
sentences.l: First the son of Hyrtacus thus with his mouth spoke:
sentences.i: The son of Hyrtacus spoke first:
sentences.n: 'Prior', 'first', the first of the two to speak. 'Hyrtacides', 'son of Hyrtacus', Nisus, the patronymic again (as at 9.234). 'sic ore locutus (est)', 'thus spoke with his mouth', the epic fullness of 'ore'; 'est' is left out, as so often with the perfect participle. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Euryale, audendum dextra; nunc ipsa vocat res.
Hac iter est.
sentences.l:
“Euryalus, it must be dared with the right hand; now the thing itself calls.
This way the road is.
sentences.i: “Euryalus, now is the time for a bold hand; the moment itself is calling us. Our way lies here.
sentences.n: Nisus's speech (320–323), spoken low in the middle of the enemy camp. 'Euryale', vocative. 'audendum (est) dextra', 'there must be daring with the right hand', the impersonal gerundive of obligation; 'dextra', ablative of means, the sword hand. 'ipsa… res', 'the situation itself', the opportunity. 'Hac iter est', 'by this way is the road', 'hac' (sc. 'via') an adverb: straight through the sleeping enemy. Elision 'Euryal(e) audendum'.

sentences.i: You keep watch and look out far afield, so that no band can rise against us from behind; I will lay all this waste and lead you through by a wide road.”
sentences.n: 'ne qua manus… possit', a purpose clause, 'so that no band may be able'; 'qua' = 'aliqua' after 'ne', as after 'si' and 'num'. 'se attollere', 'to raise itself', get up and attack. 'nobis', dative of disadvantage, 'against us'. 'custodi et consule longe', 'keep guard and take thought far off', watch the distance. 'vasta dabo' = 'vastabo', 'I will make waste', 'do' with a predicate adjective. 'lato… limite', 'by a broad path', framing 'te': the path he will cut through the sleepers. The roles follow Iliad 10, where Diomedes does the killing and Odysseus drags the dead aside and takes the horses. Nisus's speech ends. Elisions 's(e) attollere', 'custod(i) et', 'dab(o) et'.

sentences.t:
Sic memorat vocemque premit; simul ense superbum
Rhamnetem adgreditur, qui forte tapetibus altis
exstructus toto proflabat pectore somnum.
sentences.l:
So he speaks and checks his voice; at the same time with the sword proud
Rhamnes he attacks, who as it chanced on rugs, high
piled, with his whole chest was breathing out sleep.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and fell silent, and at once went at proud Rhamnes with his sword. Rhamnes lay propped high on heaped-up rugs, breathing out sleep from the depths of his chest.
sentences.n: 'memorat', 'says', the vivid present. 'vocem premit', 'checks his voice', falls silent. 'simul', 'at the same moment', the word and the stroke together. 'superbum', 'proud', for his rank: he is a king (327). 'Rhamnetem', from 'Rhamnes'. 'tapetibus altis exstructus', 'built up on high rugs', 'tapete' a Greek word for a woven coverlet, a luxury in a camp. 'toto proflabat pectore somnum', 'was breathing out sleep with his whole chest', deep in it. Rhesus in Iliad 10 is breathing hard in his sleep when Diomedes kills him, with an evil dream standing over his head (10.494–497). Elision 'Rhamnet(em) adgreditur'.

sentences.t:
Rex idem et regi Turno gratissimus augur,
sed non augurio potuit depellere pestem.
sentences.l:
A king, the same man, and to King Turnus a most welcome augur,
but not by augury could he drive off destruction.
sentences.i: He was a king, and King Turnus's best-loved augur as well, but no augury of his could keep off his doom.
sentences.n: 'Rex idem et… augur', 'a king, and the same man an augur', 'idem' marking two roles in one person, as with Anius at 3.80, 'rex Anius, rex idem hominum Phoebique sacerdos'. 'regi Turno', dative with 'gratissimus'. 'augurio', 'by augury', the reading of birds: the man who read the future for others could not see his own. The turn comes from the Iliad's catalogue of Trojan allies, where the augur Ennomus 'did not ward off black death with his birds' (2.858–859). 'pestem', 'ruin', 'death'. Elision 'id(em) et'.

sentences.i: Three of his attendants lying anyhow among the weapons near by, and Remus's armour-bearer, and his charioteer, whom he caught right under the horses, he fell upon, and with his blade sliced through their lolling necks;
sentences.n: 'Tris… iacentis', accusative plural in '-is' again, framing the line. 'temere', 'at random', anyhow, as they had dropped asleep. 'Remi', a Rutulian chief, otherwise unknown (not the Remus of Rome). 'premit', 'overpowers', with all three objects (the attendants, the armour-bearer, the charioteer). 'sub ipsis… equis', 'under the very horses', framing 'nanctus'; 'nanctus' is Greenough's form of 'nactus', from 'nanciscor', 'come upon' (the Latin Library prints 'nactus'). 'pendentia colla', 'drooping necks', heads hanging in sleep. Elision 'temer(e) inter'.

sentences.t:
tum caput ipsi aufert domino truncumque relinquit
sanguine singultantem;
sentences.l:
then the head from the master himself he takes, and the trunk leaves
with blood sobbing;
sentences.i: then he struck the head from the master himself, and left the trunk spurting blood in gasps;
sentences.n: 'ipsi… domino', 'from the master himself', Remus, the dative with 'aufero' (to take away from someone). 'truncum', 'the trunk', the headless body. 'sanguine singultantem', 'sobbing with blood', the blood pumping out in gulps like sobs; the two words take up the first half of the line, and their repeated 's' and 'n' sounds go with it. Virgil gives the picture and the sound and makes no comment. Elisions 'ips(i) aufert', 'singultant(em) atro' (across the semicolon, into the next clause).

sentences.t:
atro tepefacta cruore
terra torique madent.
sentences.l:
warmed with black gore
the earth and the couches are drenched.
sentences.i: the ground and the couches, warm with dark blood, were soaked through.
sentences.n: 'atro… cruore', 'with black gore', framing 'tepefacta', 'made warm', which agrees with the nearer subject, 'terra', but goes in sense with both; 'cruor' is blood that has been shed, 'sanguis' blood in the body. 'tori', 'couches', the beds of rugs the Rutulians lay on. 'madent', 'are wet'. The elision 'singultant(em) atro' binds this clause to the last. No other elisions.

sentences.t:
Nec non Lamyrumque Lamumque
et iuvenem Serranum, illa qui plurima nocte
luserat, insignis facie, multoque iacebat
membra deo victus:
sentences.l:
And also Lamyrus and Lamus
and the young Serranus, who that night very much
had played, outstanding in looks, and by much lay
in limbs by the god overcome:
sentences.i: Lamyrus too, and Lamus, and young Serranus, handsome to look on, who had spent most of that night at play and lay with his limbs mastered by deep draughts of the god:
sentences.n: 'Nec non', 'and not not', 'and also', with the verb ('premit', 'overpowers') carried over from 330. 'Lamyrumque Lamumque', the double '-que… -que', a jingling pair of names that are only names. 'Serranum', a name with a Roman ring: Serranus was a surname of the Atilii, and Anchises shows one of them sowing his furrow in the parade of Roman heroes (6.844). 'illa… plurima nocte', 'very much (of) that night', ablative of time; 'luserat', 'had played', probably at dice. 'insignis facie', 'striking in his looks'. 'multo… deo victus', 'overcome by much god', that is, by much wine: the god is Bacchus, his name standing for his gift. 'membra', accusative of respect (the 'Greek accusative'), 'overcome as to his limbs'. Elision 'Serran(um) illa'.

sentences.t:
felix, si protinus illum
aequasset nocti ludum in lucemque tulisset.
sentences.l:
fortunate, if straight on that
game he had made equal to the night and into the light had carried it.
sentences.i: a lucky man, had he only made his game last as long as the night and played on into the daylight.
sentences.n: 'felix (fuisset)', '(he would have been) fortunate', the conclusion of a past unreal condition with its verb left out. 'protinus', 'on and on', without a break. 'aequasset' = 'aequavisset', the syncopated pluperfect subjunctive; 'nocti', dative with 'aequo', 'had made the game equal to the night', kept it up all night. 'in lucem… tulisset', 'had carried (it) into the light', played till dawn: awake, he would have lived. A brief aside of pity over a victim is a Homeric habit. Elision 'lud(um) in'.

sentences.t:
Impastus ceu plena leo per ovilia turbans
(suadet enim vesana fames) manditque trahitque
molle pecus mutumque metu, fremit ore cruento:
sentences.l:
Unfed, as through full sheepfolds a lion running riot
(for urges him maddened hunger) both chews and drags
the soft flock, dumb with fear, roars with bloody mouth:
sentences.i: As a starving lion, driven on by the madness of hunger, runs riot through crowded sheepfolds, mauling and dragging the soft flock struck dumb with fear, and roars with blood on his jaws,
sentences.n: A lion simile, closing Nisus's killings; the next words turn it on Euryalus. 'Impastus… leo', 'an unfed lion', the adjective first and emphatic, the noun held back; 'ceu', 'as', a poetic word for 'velut'. 'plena… ovilia', 'full sheepfolds'; 'turbans', 'throwing into confusion'. The parenthesis gives the cause: 'vesana fames', 'insane hunger' (vē-sā-na, fă-mēs). 'manditque trahitque', 'both chews and drags', the double '-que'. 'mutum… metu', 'dumb with fear', the 'm' sounds running through the line. 'fremit ore cruento', 'roars with bloody jaws'. The model is Iliad 10.485–486, where Diomedes falls on the sleeping Thracians like a lion on unguarded flocks of goats or sheep. Earlier in this book Turnus prowled round the Trojan camp like a wolf at a full sheepfold, 'pleno… ovili' (9.59–64); now the Trojans are the beasts among the flock. No elisions.

sentences.t: nec minor Euryali caedes;
sentences.l: nor less (was) Euryalus's slaughter;
sentences.i: no less was the slaughter Euryalus made;
sentences.n: The simile is applied, and to both men: Nisus has been the lion, and Euryalus kills as fiercely. 'Euryali caedes', 'the slaughter of Euryalus', a subjective genitive: the killing he does, not his death. 'est' is left out. No elisions.

sentences.t:
incensus et ipse
perfurit ac multam in medio sine nomine plebem,
Fadumque Herbesumque subit Rhoetumque Abarimque,
ignaros, Rhoetum vigilantem et cuncta videntem,
sed magnum metuens se post cratera tegebat;
sentences.l:
inflamed he too
rages through, and a great, in the middle, without name, common crowd,
and Fadus and Herbesus he comes upon, and Rhoetus and Abaris,
unaware — Rhoetus awake and all things seeing,
but, greatly fearing, himself behind the mixing-bowl he was hiding;
sentences.i: he too was on fire, raging through them, and came on a great nameless throng in the middle of the camp, and on Fadus and Herbesus, Rhoetus and Abaris, all unaware — all but Rhoetus, who was awake and saw everything, but in his terror was hiding behind a mixing-bowl;
sentences.n: 'incensus et ipse', 'he too inflamed'. 'perfurit', 'rages through', 'per-' intensive. 'multam… plebem', 'a large common crowd', framing 'in medio sine nomine', 'in the middle, without names': the rank and file, who die unnamed. 'subit', 'comes up on', with all the accusatives. Four names, each with its '-que', fill the line round its one verb, a Homeric habit in lists of the slain. 'ignaros', 'unaware', of what was happening. 'Rhoetum' is repeated to correct it: he alone was awake. 'magnum metuens', 'fearing greatly', 'magnum' an adverbial accusative; some join it instead with 'cratera', 'behind a great mixing-bowl'. 'post cratera', 'behind a mixing-bowl', 'cratera' a Greek accusative singular, the great bowl of the feast. Elisions 'mult(am) in', 'Fadumqu(e) Herbesumque', 'Rhoetumqu(e) Abarimque', 'vigilant(em) et'.

sentences.t:
pectore in adverso totum cui comminus ensem
condidit adsurgenti et multa morte recepit.
sentences.l:
in the breast, facing, the whole, into whom at close quarters, sword
he buried, (him) rising, and with much death took it back.
sentences.i: As Rhoetus rose, Euryalus closed with him and buried the whole sword in his breast, and drew it back with a flood of death.
sentences.n: 'cui… adsurgenti', 'into him as he rose', a connecting relative, the dative of the person affected; 'pectore in adverso', 'in the breast turned toward him', the front of the body facing the blow. 'totum… ensem', 'the whole sword', to the hilt. 'condidit', 'buried'. 'multa morte recepit', 'took it back with much death', the life pouring out after it: a bold phrase, the ablative of attendant circumstance. Elisions 'pector(e) in', 'adsurgent(i) et'.

sentences.t:
Purpuream vomit ille animam et cum sanguine mixta
vina refert moriens;
sentences.l:
His purple he vomits, he, life, and, mixed with blood,
the wine brings back, dying;
sentences.i: He spewed out his life in a crimson stream, and as he died brought up the wine mixed with his blood;
sentences.n: 'Purpuream… animam', 'his purple life', framing 'vomit ille': the life is the blood that carries it, as Homer's warriors lose their spirit with their blood. 'purpureus' covers the whole range of deep reds. 'vomit… refert', 'vomits… brings back', the wine of the feast coming up with the blood. Elisions 'ill(e) animam', 'anim(am) et'.

sentences.t: hic furto fervidus instat.
sentences.l: this one, in his stealth, hot, presses on.
sentences.i: and Euryalus, hot in his stealthy work, pressed on.
sentences.n: 'hic', 'this one', Euryalus, set against 'ille', Rhoetus. 'furto', 'in his stealth', 'furtum' theft, and so any secret deed: here killing done by stealth at night. 'fervidus', 'glowing', heated. 'instat', 'presses on'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Iamque ad Messapi socios tendebat; ibi ignem
deficere extremum et religatos rite videbat
carpere gramen equos:
sentences.l:
And now toward Messapus's comrades he was heading; there the fire
failing, the last of it, and, tethered in due order, he was seeing
cropping grass the horses:
sentences.i: And now he was making for Messapus's men; there he could see the last of the fire dying down, and the horses, duly tethered, cropping the grass:
sentences.n: 'Messapi socios', the men of Messapus, the tamer of horses and son of Neptune (7.691), who had been given charge of the watch round the Trojan camp (9.159–161); the horses suit him. 'tendebat', 'was making his way', still Euryalus. 'ignem deficere extremum', 'the fire failing at its last', accusative and infinitive after 'videbat', as is 'religatos… equos carpere gramen', 'the horses tethered… cropping grass'; 'rite', 'in due order'. In Iliad 10 it is Rhesus's horses that Odysseus drives off; these are left where they stand. Elisions 'Iamqu(e) ad', 'ib(i) ignem', 'deficer(e) extremum', 'extrem(um) et'.

sentences.t:
breviter cum talia Nisus.
sensit enim nimia caede atque cupidine ferri:
sentences.l:
when briefly thus Nisus,
for he perceived they were being carried away by excess of slaughter and desire:
sentences.i: when Nisus, who saw that they were being swept away by too much killing and too much greed, said briefly:
sentences.n: The print has 'Nisus. sensit', a full stop before a lower-case word, a misprint for 'Nisus, sensit', corrected here: 'cum talia Nisus' does not finish a sentence but begins one, and its verb is 'ait' in the next line; 354 is a parenthesis giving his reason (many editors set it in brackets). t keeps the print. 'cum talia Nisus (ait)', 'when Nisus (said) such things', 'cum' bringing in the main event after the imperfects 'tendebat… videbat' (he was going on, when…). 'breviter', 'briefly': there is no time. 'sensit enim (eos)… ferri', 'for he felt (that they) were being carried away', the subject of the infinitive left out. 'nimia caede atque cupidine', 'by too much slaughter and desire', the greed for killing and for spoil that will undo them. Elision 'caed(e) atque'.

sentences.t:
“Absistamus, ait, nam lux inimica propinquat.
Poenarum exhaustum satis est, via facta per hostis.”
sentences.l:
“Let us stand off,” he says, “for the light, unfriendly, is approaching.
Of punishment drained enough there is; a way has been made through the enemy.”
sentences.i: “Let us stop,” he said, “for the hostile daylight is drawing near. We have taken vengeance enough, and cut our road through the enemy.”
sentences.n: Nisus's speech. Greenough prints 'ait' inside the speech with no marks round it, as he does elsewhere; this is his habit, not a slip, and t keeps it; l and i set the marks in the English way. 'Absistamus', 'let us stand off', hortatory subjunctive. 'lux inimica', 'unfriendly light', the dawn, the enemy of men who need the dark. 'Poenarum exhaustum satis est', 'enough of punishment has been drained', 'exhaustum' a neuter participle used as a noun, with the partitive genitive 'poenarum': they have drunk their fill of vengeance. 'via facta (est)', 'a way has been made', as Nisus promised (323). 'hostis', accusative plural. Elision 'Poenar(um) exhaustum'.

sentences.t:
Multa virum solido argento perfecta relinquunt
armaque craterasque simul pulchrosque tapetas.
sentences.l:
Many things of the men, of solid silver finished, they leave behind,
and arms and mixing-bowls together and beautiful rugs.
sentences.i: They left behind many things belonging to the soldiers, wrought of solid silver, and armour, and mixing-bowls, and fine rugs.
sentences.n: 'Multa virum… perfecta', 'many (objects) of the men, finished in solid silver', 'virum' = 'virorum', the old genitive plural (as 'divom', 'Teucrum'). 'relinquunt', 'they leave behind': restraint, but not for long. 'armaque craterasque… pulchrosque', '-que' three times, piling up the loot; 'crateras' and 'tapetas', Greek accusative plurals in '-as'. Elision 'solid(o) argento'.

sentences.t:
Euryalus phaleras Rhamnetis et aurea bullis
cingula,
sentences.l:
Euryalus the medallions of Rhamnes and golden with studs
the belt,
sentences.i: Euryalus took the medallions of Rhamnes and his belt, golden and set with studs —
sentences.n: 'Euryalus' is the subject, held back from its verb 'rapit' until four lines below; between come the history of the belt and a bracketed line (363). 'phaleras', 'medallions', the metal discs worn on the chest as military decorations or hung on a horse's harness, a Greek word. 'aurea bullis cingula', 'a belt golden with studs', 'bullis' ablative of respect, 'golden in its studs', that is, with golden bosses; the plural 'cingula' for one belt (as 'cristae' for one helmet's plumes); 'bulla', a boss or knob. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Tiburti Remulo ditissimus olim
quae mittit dona hospitio cum iungeret absens
Caedicus, ille suo moriens dat habere nepoti,
[post mortem bello Rutuli pugnaque potiti]
haec rapit atque umeris nequiquam fortibus aptat.
sentences.l:
to Tiburtine Remulus, very rich, once
which sends as gifts, when in guest-friendship he was joining him, absent,
Caedicus; he, dying, gives to his grandson to have;
[after his death the Rutulians in war and battle got possession;]
these he snatches, and to his shoulders, strong in vain, fits.
sentences.i: the gifts that Caedicus, a very wealthy man, once sent to Remulus of Tibur, when he pledged him friendship from afar, and that Remulus, dying, left to his grandson [and that after the grandson's death the Rutulians won in war and battle] — these he snatched up and fitted on his shoulders, strong to no purpose.
sentences.n: Line 363 is bracketed by Greenough as spurious and kept here inside [ ]: it reads like a note explaining how a Rutulian came to own the belt; without it, Rhamnes is the grandson. 'Tiburti Remulo', 'to Remulus of Tibur' (Tivoli), dative. 'quae… dona', 'which gifts', the relative clause set before its subject 'Caedicus'. 'ditissimus', superlative of 'dis', 'rich'. 'mittit… dat', vivid presents. 'hospitio cum iungeret absens', 'when, absent, he was joining (him) in guest-friendship', bound by gifts though they never met, a Homeric custom (Glaucus and Diomedes, Iliad 6). 'ille', Remulus; 'dat habere', 'gives to have', a poetic infinitive of purpose. 'haec rapit', 'these he snatches'. 'nequiquam fortibus', 'strong in vain': the spoils will help to kill him, as the belt Turnus strips from Pallas (10.495–500) will kill Turnus. Elisions 'don(a) hospitio', 'atqu(e) umeris'.

sentences.t:
Tum galeam Messapi habilem cristisque decoram
induit. Excedunt castris et tuta capessunt.
sentences.l:
Then the helmet of Messapus, well-fitting and with crests handsome,
he puts on. They go out of the camp and safe ground make for.
sentences.i: Then he put on Messapus's helmet, close-fitting and handsome with its plumes. They left the camp and made for safety.
sentences.n: 'Messapi', genitive: the helmet lay among Messapus's men, perhaps the chief's own. 'habilem', 'handy', fitting him well; 'cristis decoram', 'handsome with its crests'. 'induit', 'puts on', the verb held over to the next line for emphasis: this is the helmet that will betray him (373–374). 'tuta', 'safe places', a neuter plural adjective as noun; 'capessunt', 'make for', from 'capesso', to seize eagerly. Elision 'Messap(i) habilem'.

sentences.t:
Interea praemissi equites ex urbe Latina,
cetera dum legio campis instructa moratur,
ibant et Turno regi responsa ferebant,
tercentum, scutati omnes, Volcente magistro.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile, horsemen sent ahead from the Latin city,
while the rest of the legion, on the plains drawn up, waits,
were going, and to Turnus the king answers were bringing,
three hundred, shield-bearing all, Volcens commanding.
sentences.i: Meanwhile horsemen sent on ahead from the Latin city, while the rest of the force waited drawn up on the plain, were on their way with answers for King Turnus: three hundred of them, every man with his long shield, under the command of Volcens.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough. 'praemissi equites', 'horsemen sent ahead', from Laurentum, Latinus's city. 'cetera… legio', 'the rest of the legion', a Roman word for the Latin force; 'dum… moratur', 'while (it) waits', 'dum' with the present indicative even in past narrative. 'responsa', 'answers', to messages Turnus had sent: what they were is never said. 'tercentum', 'three hundred' (the Latin Library prints 'ter centum'). 'scutati', 'armed with the scutum', the long body-shield. 'Volcente magistro', ablative absolute, 'Volcens (being) commander'. Elisions 'praemiss(i) equites', 'scutat(i) omnes'.

sentences.t:
Iamque propinquabant castris murosque subibant,
cum procul hos laevo flectentis limite cernunt
et galea Euryalum sublustri noctis in umbra
prodidit immemorem radiisque adversa refulsit.
sentences.l:
And now they were nearing the camp and coming up to the walls,
when far off these two, by a path on the left turning, they see,
and the helmet Euryalus in the half-lit shadow of night
betrayed, forgetful, and, facing the rays, flashed back.
sentences.i: They were already nearing the camp and coming up under the walls when they caught sight of the two far off, turning away by a path on the left; and in the glimmering dark of night the helmet betrayed Euryalus, who had forgotten it, flashing back where the moonlight struck it.
sentences.n: 'castris… muros', the Rutulian camp and the walls of the Trojan camp it besieges. 'cum… cernunt', 'when they see', 'cum' bringing in the turn of the story, with the vivid present. 'hos… flectentis', 'these men turning', 'flectentis' accusative plural; 'laevo… limite', 'by a path on the left'. 'galea… prodidit', 'the helmet betrayed', a new subject and the past tense. 'sublustri', 'faintly lit', a rare word; 'immemorem', 'forgetful', of the bright helmet on his head. 'radiis adversa', 'facing the rays', of the moon, to whom Nisus will pray (403); 'refulsit', 'flashed back'. Elisions 'gale(a) Euryalum', 'radiisqu(e) adversa'.

sentences.t: Haud temere est visum.
sentences.l: Not idly was it seen.
sentences.i: The sight was not lost on them.
sentences.n: 'Haud temere est visum', 'not idly was it seen', an impersonal passive: the horsemen took note, and acted. A short sentence after a long one marks the turn. Elision 'temer(e) est' (or 'temere 'st').

sentences.t:
Conclamat ab agmine Volcens
“State, viri. Quae causa viae? Quive estis in armis?
Quove tenetis iter? ”Nihil illi tendere contra,
sed celerare fugam in silvas et fidere nocti.
sentences.l:
Shouts out from the column Volcens:
“Stand, men. What is the reason for your road? Or who are you, in arms?
Or where are you holding your way?” Nothing they in return,
but to hasten flight into the woods and to trust the night.
sentences.i: Volcens shouted from the column: “Halt, men! What is your business on the road? Who are you, under arms? Where are you heading?” They made no answer, but ran for the woods and trusted to the night.
sentences.n: The print has 'iter? ”Nihil', a misprint for 'iter?” Nihil', corrected here: the closing mark is set after the space and joined to the next word (as at 7.68 and 8.113); t keeps the print, so this unit runs on to the end of the narrative sentence. 'Conclamat', 'calls out', 'con-' of a loud shout; 'ab agmine', 'from the column'. Volcens's challenge is three short questions, a sentry's challenge. 'State', 'stand', halt. 'Quive… Quove', 'or who… or where', '-ve' joining the questions. 'Nihil illi tendere contra', 'they (made) no move in return', and 'celerare… fidere', '(they) hastened… trusted': historical infinitives, the infinitive standing for a main verb in quick narrative, with its subject in the nominative (you will meet these often). 'tendere contra', 'to strive back', answer or resist. Elisions 'Quiv(e) estis', 'fug(am) in'.

sentences.t:
Obiciunt equites sese ad divortia nota
hinc atque hinc omnemque abitum custode coronant.
sentences.l:
Throw the horsemen themselves across the branchings, well known,
on this side and that, and every way out with guards they ring.
sentences.i: The horsemen threw themselves across the forks of the road they knew, on either side, and ringed every way out with guards.
sentences.n: 'Obiciunt… sese', 'throw themselves in the way'. 'divortia nota', 'the well-known turnings', where the tracks part; the horsemen are local men. 'hinc atque hinc', 'on this side and on that'. 'omnem… abitum', 'every way out'; the Latin Library prints 'aditum', 'every approach', the same cordon seen from outside. 'custode', a collective singular, 'with guards'; 'coronant', 'ring', as a crown rings the head. Elisions 'ses(e) ad', 'atqu(e) hinc', 'omnemqu(e) abitum'.

sentences.i: There was a wood spreading wide, rough with brushwood and dark holm-oak, choked on every side with thick-set thorns; only here and there a path showed faintly along the hidden tracks.
sentences.n: A set description of a place, opening as such descriptions do with 'there was' ('silva fuit', like 'est locus'). 'late… horrida', 'bristling far and wide', with 'dumis atque ilice nigra', 'with brambles and black ilex', the evergreen holm-oak, dark with shade. 'complerant' = 'compleverant', the syncopated pluperfect. 'sentes', 'thorn-bushes'. 'rara… semita', 'a scattered path', a path showing only here and there; 'per occultos… calles', 'through hidden tracks', 'callis' a narrow footpath, often a cattle-track. Elision 'atqu(e) ilice'.

sentences.t:
Euryalum tenebrae ramorum onerosaque praeda
impediunt fallitque timor regione viarum;
sentences.l:
Euryalus the darkness of the branches and the burdensome booty
hinder, and fear deceives him in the direction of the ways;
sentences.i: Euryalus was hampered by the darkness under the branches and the weight of his plunder, and fear led him astray in the tangle of the paths;
sentences.n: 'Euryalum', the object, first and emphatic. 'onerosa praeda', 'the burdensome booty': the price of his spoils is paid at once. 'fallit… regione viarum', 'deceives (him) in the direction of the ways', makes him mistake the line of the paths; 'regione' ablative of respect. Elision 'ramor(um) onerosaque' (rā-mō-rum, ŏ-nĕ-rō-sa).

sentences.t:
Nisus abit, iamque imprudens evaserat hostis
atque locos, qui post Albae de nomine dicti
Albani, tum rex stabula alta Latinus habebat,
ut stetit et frustra absentem respexit amicum.
sentences.l:
Nisus gets away; and now, unawares, he had escaped the enemy
and the places which afterwards, from the name of Alba, called
Alban (were) — then King Latinus high stalls kept there —
when he stood still and in vain looked back for his absent friend.
sentences.i: Nisus got clear. Without realising it he had already left the enemy behind, and the ground later called Alban after the name of Alba, where in those days King Latinus kept his tall cattle-pens, when he stopped, and looked back in vain for his missing friend.
sentences.n: 'abit', 'gets away', the present; 'iamque… evaserat', 'and now he had escaped', the pluperfect showing how far he had gone before he noticed. 'imprudens', 'unawares', not knowing that Euryalus was no longer behind him. 'hostis', accusative plural. 'locos… dicti Albani', 'the places afterward called Alban', 'Albae de nomine', from the name of Alba Longa, the city Ascanius is to found (1.267–271): Virgil sets his story on ground his readers knew, the Alban hills south-east of Rome. 'tum', 'at that time'; 'stabula alta', 'tall stalls', cattle-pens: Latinus is a king of herdsmen. 'ut stetit', 'when he stopped', 'ut' temporal with the perfect. 'absentem… amicum', 'his absent friend', framing 'respexit'. Elisions 'iamqu(e) imprudens', 'stabul(a) alta', 'frustr(a) absentem'.

sentences.t: “Euryale infelix, qua te regione reliqui?
sentences.l: “Euryalus, unlucky one, in what quarter have I left you?
sentences.i: “Euryalus, my ill-starred friend, where was it I left you?
sentences.n: Nisus's cry (390–392), to himself. 'infelix', 'ill-starred', an epithet of pity. 'qua… regione', 'in what quarter', ablative of place. 'reliqui', 'did I leave', with the sting of 'abandon'. 'Euryale' has the Greek 'eu' as one long syllable, and its final 'e' is elided before 'infelix': Eu-ry-a-l(e) in-fe-lix. Elision 'Euryal(e) infelix'.

sentences.t:
Quave sequar, rursus perplexum iter omne revolvens
fallacis silvae? ”Simul et vestigia retro
observata legit dumisque silentibus errat.
sentences.l:
Or by what way shall I follow, again the tangled route, all of it, unwinding
of the deceitful wood?” At once, too, his footprints backward
watched for he gathers up, and among the silent thickets wanders.
sentences.i: Which way am I to follow, unwinding again the whole tangled path of this treacherous wood?” With that he went back, picking out his own footprints as he watched for them, and wandered through the silent thickets.
sentences.n: The print has 'silvae? ”Simul', a misprint for 'silvae?” Simul', corrected here: again the closing mark is joined to the next word; t keeps the print, and the unit runs on to 'errat.'. 'Quave sequar', 'or by what way am I to follow?', a deliberative subjunctive. 'rursus… revolvens', 'unrolling again', retracing, as a thread is wound back; 'perplexum iter omne… fallacis silvae', 'the whole tangled route of the deceiving wood'. 'Simul et', 'at the same time too': he speaks and acts together. 'vestigia retro observata legit', 'he gathers up his footprints backward, watched for', traces his own tracks back with his eyes on the ground; 'lego' of following a path, as of reading. 'dumis silentibus', 'among the silent thickets', ablative of place: the silence before the noise of 394. Elision 'perplex(um) iter'.

sentences.t: Audit equos, audit strepitus et signa sequentum.
sentences.l: He hears horses, he hears the din and the signals of pursuers.
sentences.i: He heard horses, he heard the clatter and the calls of the pursuers.
sentences.n: 'Audit… audit', the verb repeated (anaphora) as the sounds break in on him. 'strepitus', plural, 'noises'; 'signa', 'signals', calls or shouted orders. 'sequentum' = 'sequentium', 'of those pursuing', the participle's genitive plural in '-um'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Nec longum in medio tempus, cum clamor ad auris
pervenit ac videt Euryalum, quem iam manus omnis
fraude loci et noctis, subito turbante tumultu,
oppressum rapit et conantem plurima frustra.
sentences.l:
Nor long (was) the time between, when a shout to his ears
came, and he sees Euryalus, whom now the band entire,
by the treachery of the place and of night, a sudden uproar confusing him,
overpowered is carrying off, and trying very many things in vain.
sentences.i: It was not long before a shout reached his ears, and he saw Euryalus: betrayed by the place and the darkness, thrown into confusion by the sudden uproar, he had been overpowered by the whole troop and was being dragged away, struggling hard and all in vain.
sentences.n: 'Nec longum in medio tempus (erat)', 'nor (was there) a long time between', the verb left out. 'cum… pervenit', 'when (a shout) reached', 'cum' bringing in the event again; 'pervenit' is present (pervĕnit, as the metre shows), like 'videt'. 'auris', accusative plural. 'manus omnis', 'the whole band'. 'fraude loci et noctis', 'by the treachery of the place and the night', the wood and the dark they had trusted (378) turning against him. 'subito turbante tumultu', ablative absolute, 'a sudden uproar confusing (him)'. 'oppressum rapit', 'is carrying off overpowered', the participle doing the work of a second verb. 'conantem plurima frustra', 'trying very many things in vain'. Elisions 'long(um) in', 'loc(i) et'.

sentences.t:
Quid faciat? Qua vi iuvenem, quibus audeat armis
eripere?
sentences.l:
What is he to do? By what force the young man, with what arms should he dare
to snatch away?
sentences.i: What was he to do? With what force, with what weapons could he dare to snatch the young man free?
sentences.n: Nisus's thoughts are given as questions in the deliberative subjunctive ('faciat', 'audeat'), the narrator speaking from inside his mind. 'Qua vi… quibus… armis', 'by what force, with what arms', the question word doubled: he is one man against three hundred. 'eripere', 'to snatch away', rescue. Elision 'eriper(e) An' (across the question mark, into the next unit).

sentences.t:
An sese medios moriturus in enses
inferat et pulchram properet per volnera mortem?
sentences.l:
Or himself into the midst, to die, of the swords
should he bear, and hasten through wounds a beautiful death?
sentences.i: Or should he hurl himself into the thick of their swords to die, and rush through wounds to a glorious death?
sentences.n: 'An', 'or', bringing in the second alternative. 'sese… inferat', 'should he carry himself into', charge; 'medios… in enses', 'into the midst of the swords', framing 'moriturus', 'meaning to die', the future participle of purpose. 'pulchram… mortem', 'a fine death', framing 'properet per volnera': the old ideal of a glorious death in arms, as on the night Troy fell Aeneas thought 'pulchrumque mori succurrit in armis' (2.317). 'properet… mortem', 'hasten on death', 'propero' used transitively. 'volnera', Greenough's spelling of 'vulnera'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ocius adducto torquens hastile lacerto,
suspiciens altam Lunam sic voce precatur:
sentences.l:
Quickly, with arm drawn back, poising a spear-shaft,
looking up at the high Moon, thus with his voice he prays:
sentences.i: Quickly he drew back his arm and poised a javelin, and looking up at the Moon riding high, he prayed aloud:
sentences.n: 'Ocius', 'more swiftly', the comparative meaning 'at once'. 'adducto… lacerto', ablative absolute, 'the arm drawn back'; 'torquens hastile', 'brandishing a shaft', poising it to throw. Greenough's 'torquens' makes 'precatur' the only main verb; the Latin Library prints 'torquet' (with 'et' in 403), two main verbs, 'he poises his spear and, looking up…, prays': the picture is the same. 'suspiciens', 'looking up at'. 'altam Lunam', 'the Moon on high', the moon that betrayed Euryalus's helmet (374); the Moon is Diana, goddess of the hunt and of the night. No elisions.

sentences.t:
“Tu, dea, tu praesens nostro succurre labori,
astrorum decus et nemorum Latonia custos.
sentences.l:
“You, goddess, you, present, to our trouble come to aid,
glory of the stars, and of the groves, daughter of Latona, guardian.
sentences.i: “You, goddess, be with us now and help us in our need, glory of the stars, daughter of Latona, guardian of the woods.
sentences.n: Nisus's prayer (404–409) has the shape of a Roman prayer: the god called by her titles, the claim on her favour ('if ever…'), and the request. 'Tu… tu', the pronoun repeated, as in hymns. 'praesens', 'present', the word for a god who is at hand and acts. 'labori', 'trouble', distress, dative with 'succurre'. 'astrorum decus', 'ornament of the stars', as the Moon; 'nemorum… custos', 'guardian of the groves', as Diana the huntress; 'Latonia', 'daughter of Latona' (the Greek Leto), mother of Apollo and Diana. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Siqua tuis umquam pro me pater Hyrtacus aris
dona tulit, siqua ipse meis venatibus auxi
suspendive tholo aut sacra ad fastigia fixi:
sentences.l:
If any to your altars ever on my behalf my father Hyrtacus
gifts brought, if any I myself from my hunting have added
or hung from the dome or to the sacred gables fastened,
sentences.i: If ever my father Hyrtacus brought gifts to your altars on my behalf, if ever I have added to them from my own hunting, hanging them from your dome or nailing them to your holy gable,
sentences.n: 'Siqua… siqua', 'if any (gifts)', = 'si qua', Greenough printing them as one word (the Latin Library divides them). This is the claim on the god's favour, as old as Chryses's prayer to Apollo in Iliad 1.39–41, 'if ever I roofed a temple pleasing to you…'. 'pro me', 'for me', on my behalf, when I was a child. 'meis venatibus auxi', 'I have added from my own hunting', increased the gifts: the hunter dedicates heads, horns and skins to Diana. 'suspendive tholo', 'or hung from the dome', '-ve' 'or'; 'tholus', a Greek word, the round vaulted roof of a temple. 'sacra ad fastigia', 'to the sacred gable', the pediment, where trophies were nailed. Elisions 'siqu(a) ipse', 'thol(o) aut', 'sacr(a) ad'.

sentences.t: hunc sine me turbare globum et rege tela per auras.”
sentences.l: this let me throw into disorder, the knot, and guide my weapons through the air.”
sentences.i: then let me throw this mass of men into disorder, and guide my weapons through the air.”
sentences.n: The request. 'sine me turbare', 'allow me to throw into disorder', 'sine' the imperative of 'sino' (as at 9.291). 'hunc… globum', 'this mass', the knot of horsemen round Euryalus, framing the verb. 'rege tela', 'guide my weapons': he throws in the dark and cannot see where they land. Nisus's prayer ends. Elision 'glob(um) et'.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, et toto conixus corpore ferrum
conicit:
sentences.l:
He had spoken, and with his whole body straining the steel
he hurls:
sentences.i: He had finished speaking, and straining with his whole body he hurled the iron-tipped shaft:
sentences.n: 'Dixerat', 'he had spoken', the pluperfect closing the speech, a standing formula. 'toto conixus corpore', 'straining with his whole body', 'conixus' from 'conitor' (Greenough's spelling; 'conisus' in many texts). 'ferrum', 'the iron', the spear named by its point. 'conicit', 'hurls', held over to the next line; 'conixus… conicit' is a play of sounds. No elisions.

sentences.t:
hasta volans noctis diverberat umbras
et venit aversi in tergum Sulmonis ibique
frangitur ac fisso transit praecordia ligno.
sentences.l:
the spear, flying, of the night beats apart the shadows,
and comes, of the turned-away, into the back of Sulmo, and there
is broken, and with the wood split passes through his vitals.
sentences.i: the spear flew, cleaving the shadows of the night, and struck Sulmo in the back as he faced the other way; there it snapped, and the splintered shaft passed on through his chest.
sentences.n: 'diverberat umbras', 'beats the shadows apart', 'di-' 'asunder': the spear cuts through the darkness. 'aversi… Sulmonis', 'of Sulmo, turned away', framing 'in tergum'; he was facing the other way, toward Euryalus. 'ibique frangitur', 'and there it is broken', the shaft snapping with the blow; 'fisso… ligno', ablative absolute, 'the wood split', and still the point drives on. 'praecordia', 'the parts before the heart', the midriff and chest. Elision 'avers(i) in'.

sentences.t:
Volvitur ille vomens calidum de pectore flumen
frigidus et longis singultibus ilia pulsat.
sentences.l:
Rolls over he, vomiting a hot from his breast stream,
cold, and with long sobs his flanks beats.
sentences.i: He rolled over, pouring a hot stream from his chest, himself already cold, and his flanks heaved with long gasping sobs.
sentences.n: 'Volvitur', 'rolls over', the dying fall. 'calidum… flumen', 'a warm river', of blood, framing 'de pectore'; 'frigidus', 'cold', set first in the next line against it: the warm blood leaves the body as it grows cold. 'longis singultibus', 'with long sobs', the death-rattle (as 'singultantem', 333); 'ilia', 'flanks'; 'pulsat', 'beats', heaves. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Diversi circumspiciunt. Hoc acrior idem
ecce aliud summa telum librabat ab aure.
sentences.l:
In different directions they look round. By this the keener, the same man,
look, another, from the top of his ear, weapon was poising.
sentences.i: They looked round this way and that. Fiercer for his success, there he was again, poising another spear high by his ear.
sentences.n: 'Diversi', 'in different directions', each looking his own way; 'circumspiciunt', five syllables, with 'Diversi' fills the line up to the main pause in the fourth foot. 'Hoc acrior', 'the keener for this', 'hoc' ablative of cause or of the degree of difference. 'idem', 'the same man', Nisus. 'ecce', 'look!', drawing the reader into the scene. 'aliud… telum', 'another weapon', framing 'summa'; 'summa… ab aure', 'from the top of his ear', from high by his ear, the throwing position. 'librabat', 'was poising', balancing it to throw. Elision 'ecc(e) aliud'.

sentences.t:
Dum trepidant, it hasta Tago per tempus utrumque
stridens traiectoque haesit tepefacta cerebro.
sentences.l:
While they are in alarm, goes the spear, for Tagus, through temple, each,
whistling, and in the pierced stuck, warmed, brain.
sentences.i: While they were in confusion, the spear went hissing through both of Tagus's temples and stuck, warm, in the brain it had pierced.
sentences.n: 'Dum trepidant', 'while they are in alarm', 'dum' with the present. 'Tago', dative of the person affected, 'for Tagus'; 'per tempus utrumque', 'through both temples', in at one side and out at the other. 'stridens', 'hissing', the sound of the spear in flight. 'traiecto… cerebro', 'in the pierced brain', framing 'haesit tepefacta', 'stuck, warmed'. Elision 'traiectoqu(e) haesit'.

sentences.t:
Saevit atrox Volcens nec teli conspicit usquam
auctorem nec quo se ardens inmittere possit.
sentences.l:
Rages, fierce, Volcens, nor of the weapon sees anywhere
the author, nor where himself, blazing, to hurl he can.
sentences.i: Volcens raged in savage fury, but could see nowhere the man who had thrown the spear, nor anywhere to hurl himself in his anger.
sentences.n: 'Saevit atrox', 'rages, savage', verb and adjective side by side. 'nec… nec', 'neither… nor'. 'teli… auctorem', 'the author of the weapon', the thrower. 'quo se… inmittere possit', 'where he could fling himself', an indirect question; 'ardens', 'blazing', with rage. 'inmittere', Greenough's 'inm-' for 'imm-'. Elision 's(e) ardens'.

sentences.t:
“Tu tamen interea calido mihi sanguine poenas
persolves amborum, ”inquit;
sentences.l:
“You, however, meanwhile, with warm blood to me the penalty
shall pay for both,” he says;
sentences.i: “You, at least, shall pay me for the two of them with your warm blood in the meantime,” he said;
sentences.n: The print has 'amborum, ”inquit', a misprint for 'amborum,” inquit', corrected here: the closing mark is joined to the next word (as at 377 and 392); t keeps the print. Volcens turns on the prisoner. 'Tu tamen', 'you, however', you at least, since the thrower cannot be found. 'interea', 'meanwhile', until the other is caught. 'calido… sanguine', 'with warm blood', framing 'mihi', the dative of the person to whom the penalty is paid. 'poenas persolves', 'you will pay the penalty in full', 'poenas' held over to the next line; 'amborum', 'for both', Sulmo and Tagus, a genitive with 'poenas', the penalty owed for them. Elision 'ambor(um) inquit'.

sentences.t:
simul ense recluso
ibat in Euryalum.
sentences.l:
at the same time, with sword unsheathed,
he was going at Euryalus.
sentences.i: and with that he drew his sword and went for Euryalus.
sentences.n: 'simul', 'at the same moment'. 'ense recluso', ablative absolute, 'the sword unsheathed', 'recludo', 'open up', of drawing a blade from its sheath. 'ibat in', 'was going at', the imperfect of an act begun and not finished: what follows happens while he is moving. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Tum vero exterritus, amens
conclamat Nisus, nec se celare tenebris
amplius aut tantum potuit perferre dolorem.
sentences.l:
Then indeed, terrified, out of his mind,
cries out Nisus; nor himself to hide in the darkness
any longer, or so great could he endure the grief.
sentences.i: Then indeed Nisus, terrified and out of his mind, cried out aloud; he could no longer hide himself in the darkness or endure such agony.
sentences.n: 'Tum vero', 'then indeed', marking the climax. 'exterritus, amens', 'terrified, out of his mind', two adjectives without a connective. 'conclamat', 'cries aloud', as Volcens 'conclamat' at 375. 'nec… potuit', 'nor could he', with two infinitives, 'celare' and 'perferre'; 'tenebris', 'in the darkness', ablative of place. 'tantum… dolorem', 'so great a grief', framing 'potuit perferre'. Elision 'ver(o) exterritus'.

sentences.t:
Me me, adsum qui feci, in me convertite ferrum,
O Rutuli, mea fraus omnis;
sentences.l:
“Me, me — here I am, who did it — on me turn the steel,
O Rutulians; mine the deceit, all of it;
sentences.i: “Me, it is me! Here I stand, the man who did it: turn your blades against me, men of the Rutuli! All of the trickery was mine;
sentences.n: The print has 'Me me' with no opening mark, a misprint for '“Me me', corrected here: Greenough closes the speech at 430, and l and i open it here. Nisus's cry (427–430), among the most famous outbursts in the poem. 'Me me', accusatives with no verb yet: he cannot wait for one, and the thought is taken up by 'in me convertite ferrum'. 'adsum qui feci', 'here I am, the one who did it'. 'in me convertite ferrum', 'turn the steel against me'. 'mea fraus omnis (est)', 'all the trick is mine', 'fraus' the stealthy attack. Elisions 'm(e) adsum', 'fec(i) in'.

sentences.t:
nihil iste nec ausus
nec potuit, caelum hoc et conscia sidera testor,
tantum infelicem nimium dilexit amicum.”
sentences.l:
nothing he there either dared
or could do — this sky and the knowing stars I call to witness —
only his unlucky friend too much he loved.”
sentences.i: he dared nothing and had the power to do nothing — this sky and the stars that know the truth are my witnesses — his only offence was to love his ill-starred friend beyond measure.”
sentences.n: 'nihil… nec ausus (est) nec potuit', 'he neither dared nor was able (to do) anything', 'nihil' strengthened, not cancelled, by 'nec… nec', as in everyday speech. 'iste', 'that one there', the pronoun for the person near those spoken to: Euryalus is in their hands. 'caelum hoc et conscia sidera testor', 'I call to witness this sky and the stars that share the knowledge', 'conscia', 'knowing', who saw what was done; 'testor' takes the witnesses in the accusative. 'tantum… dilexit', 'he only loved', with 'infelicem… amicum' framing 'nimium', 'too much': the unlucky friend is Nisus himself. Nisus's speech ends. Elisions 'cael(um) hoc', 'tant(um) infelicem'.

sentences.t:
Talia dicta dabat; sed viribus ensis adactus
transabiit costas et candida pectora rumpit.
sentences.l:
Such words he was giving; but, with force driven, the sword
went clean through the ribs and the white breast bursts.
sentences.i: He was still crying out these words, but the sword, driven home with all the man's strength, had gone clean through the ribs and was breaking open the white breast.
sentences.n: 'Talia dicta dabat', 'such words he was giving', the imperfect: he is still speaking when it is done. 'viribus… adactus', 'driven with force', framing 'ensis'; the blow is Volcens's. 'transabiit', 'went right through', a rare compound of 'trans', 'ab' and 'eo', its perfect set beside the present 'rumpit'. The Latin Library prints 'transadigit', 'drives through', with the sword as subject, which changes the verb but not the event. 'candida pectora', 'white breast', the plural for one breast; the colour marks youth and beauty and is set against the blood of the next line. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Volvitur Euryalus leto, pulchrosque per artus
it cruor, inque umeros cervix conlapsa recumbit:
sentences.l:
Rolls over Euryalus in death, and over the beautiful limbs
goes the blood, and onto his shoulders the neck, collapsing, sinks back:
sentences.i: Down went Euryalus, rolling in death; blood streamed over his handsome limbs, and his neck, its strength gone, sank back upon his shoulders:
sentences.n: 'Volvitur… leto', 'rolls in death', the same verb as for Sulmo (414); 'leto' ablative of manner. 'pulchros… per artus', 'over his beautiful limbs', framing '-que'; 'it cruor', 'the blood goes', short and plain. 'in… umeros', 'onto his shoulders'; 'conlapsa', Greenough's 'conl-' for 'coll-', 'having given way'; 'recumbit', 'sinks back'. Elision 'inqu(e) umeros'.

sentences.t:
purpureus veluti cum flos succisus aratro
languescit moriens lassove papavera collo
demisere caput, pluvia cum forte gravantur.
sentences.l:
purple — as when a flower, cut from below by the plough,
grows faint, dying, or poppies with weary neck
have let fall their head, when by rain, as it chances, they are weighed down.
sentences.i: as a red flower, sheared off at the root by the plough, wilts away in dying, or as poppies, their stems grown weary, let their heads sink when a chance shower weighs them down.
sentences.n: The simile of the cut flower, one of the most admired in Virgil. 'purpureus… flos', 'a purple flower', framing 'veluti cum', 'as when'; the colour takes up the blood. 'succisus aratro', 'cut from beneath by the plough'. 'languescit moriens', 'grows faint, dying'. 'lasso… collo', 'with weary neck', framing 'papavera', 'poppies'; 'demisere' = 'demiserunt', 'have let fall', the perfect of what habitually happens (the gnomic perfect). 'pluvia… gravantur', 'are weighed down by rain'. Virgil joins two models: Iliad 8.306–308, where the dying Gorgythion's head droops to one side like a poppy in a garden heavy with its seed and the spring rains, and Catullus 11.22–24, where the poet's love lies fallen like a flower at the meadow's edge, touched by the passing plough. No elisions.

sentences.t:
At Nisus ruit in medios solumque per omnis
Volcentem petit in solo Volcente moratur.
sentences.l:
But Nisus rushes into the midst, and, alone, through them all
Volcens he seeks, on Volcens alone he dwells.
sentences.i: But Nisus charged into the middle of them, and through them all he sought Volcens alone, and had no thought for anyone but Volcens.
sentences.n: 'At', 'but', turning from the dead to the living. 'ruit in medios', 'rushes into the midst', as he had thought of doing (400). 'solum… Volcentem', 'Volcens alone', and then 'in solo Volcente', the same words in another case (polyptoton) at the same point of the next clause: his whole mind narrows to one man. 'per omnis', 'through all', accusative plural. 'moratur', 'lingers', will not be turned aside. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Quem circum glomerati hostes hinc comminus atque hinc
proturbant.
sentences.l:
Him around, massed, the enemy, on this side at close quarters and on this,
thrust back.
sentences.i: The enemy closed round him in a mass and beat him back hand to hand from either side.
sentences.n: 'Quem circum', 'around whom', the preposition after its object (anastrophe), a connecting relative: 'and around him'. 'glomerati', 'balled together', massed. 'hinc… atque hinc', 'on this side and that', framing 'comminus', 'hand to hand'. 'proturbant', 'drive him back', held over to the next line. Elisions 'glomerat(i) hostes', 'atqu(e) hinc'.

sentences.t:
Instat non setius ac rotat ensem
fulmineum, donec Rutuli clamantis in ore
condidit adverso et moriens animam abstulit hosti.
sentences.l:
He presses on none the less, and whirls his sword,
lightning-swift, until of the Rutulian, shouting, in the mouth
he buried it, facing him, and, dying, the life took from his enemy.
sentences.i: He pressed on none the less, whirling his flashing sword, until he buried it full in the face of the shouting Rutulian, and, dying himself, took his enemy's life.
sentences.n: 'non setius', 'none the less', 'setius' (often 'secius') a comparative adverb. 'rotat ensem fulmineum', 'whirls his flashing sword', 'fulmineus', like a thunderbolt in speed and gleam. 'donec… condidit', 'until he buried (it)', 'donec' with the perfect indicative of a thing that actually happened. 'Rutuli clamantis', 'of the shouting Rutulian', Volcens, still shouting orders. 'in ore… adverso', 'in the face turned toward him', full in the face. 'moriens animam abstulit hosti', 'dying, he took away his enemy's life', 'hosti' dative of separation: Nisus has his revenge in the moment he takes his own death-wound. Elisions 'advers(o) et', 'anim(am) abstulit'.

sentences.t:
Tum super exanimum sese proiecit amicum
confossus placidaque ibi demum morte quievit.
sentences.l:
Then upon his lifeless he flung himself friend,
pierced through, and in peaceful there at last death he rested.
sentences.i: Then, his body pierced again and again, he threw himself on his lifeless friend, and there at last a calm death brought him rest.
sentences.n: 'super exanimum… amicum', 'upon his lifeless friend', framing 'sese proiecit'. 'proiecit', 'flung himself down'. 'confossus', 'stabbed through', set first in the next line: he is already riddled with wounds. 'placida… morte', 'in calm death', framing 'ibi demum', 'there at last', an ablative of manner with 'quievit', 'came to rest': after the frenzy of the last lines the episode ends on its quietest word. The next part opens with the poet's own address to the two friends (9.446–449). Elision 'placidaqu(e) ibi'.
